Words: Alexandra Carleton

Illustrations: Kylie Silvester

Editing: Catherine Taylor

World.title: Australian taxpayers take on risk for major oil and gas projects
World.content:
Major energy companies are telling Australians that this country's oil and gas industry relies "entirely" on private sector investment.

In a recent social media post, the Australian Energy Producers made this claim:

"You might have heard the claim that Australia should tax its oil and gas industry the same way Norway does. But does that comparison really stack up?



"For starters, the Norwegian government is a major investor and co-owner of its oil and gas industry, whereas Australia’s oil and gas industry relies entirely on private sector investment. "That means, in Australia, the private sector — not government — wears all of the risk and up-front costs, which can be in the tens of billions for just one project."

In other words, the oil and gas lobby argues that Australian governments don't wear any risk in the development of our oil and gas industry and don't assume any up-front costs for major energy projects.

But do these claims stack up to scrutiny?

An industry built on help from governments

Australian Energy Producers (AEP) is the "peak" industry body representing Australia's oil and gas exploration and production sector.

Its members include Woodside Energy, Santos, Chevron, Shell, Origin, Inpex, BP, Hancock Prospecting, Exxon Mobil, and Halliburton, among others.

Woodside's North West Shelf given final approval to operate until 2070 Australia's biggest gas project, Woodside's North West Shelf, has received final approval to extend operations through until 2070.

Many of those companies have well-oiled lobbying and PR operations that have been honed over decades because they know that "help from the government" is exactly what they need.

Take the North West Shelf project, which is Australia's largest oil and gas project.

In a submission to a federal inquiry into the Petroleum Resource Rent Tax (PRRT) in 2016, Western Australia's government had this to say about the North West Shelf:

"In the 1970s and 1980s the state played a pivotal role in securing the development of the North West Shelf project through agreements, financial assistance and infrastructure provision. "If the state had not made these investments, the project would likely not have succeeded."

Woodside faces scrutiny over spill The energy giant says 16,000 litres of "hydrocarbons" spilt into the Indian Ocean north of Exmouth early this month.

It said the North West Shelf project proceeded in two major stages.

The first stage, "the domestic stage," which got the project up and running, involved the production of natural gas, which the (then) State Electricity Commission of Western Australia (SECWA) promised to purchase.

SECWA was a WA government-owned entity. And it didn't promise to purchase some of the project's early gas output. It agreed to purchase all of it.

Why would it do that? So that the North West Shelf project would have a guaranteed customer in its early years to ensure its economic viability.

As the WA government explained in its submission:

"The domestic phase was underpinned by 20-year 'take or pay' contracts, signed in September 1980, between the Project Joint Venturers and SECWA for the supply of 414 tetrajoules per day of natural gas (commencing in 1985) — the entire gas output from the domestic phase. "These state agreements were essential in ensuring the financial robustness for the North West Shelf project and were key to securing contracts with Japanese utilities for the export phase."

So, state government support was essential, in the beginning, to get the project into a position where it was capable of exporting Australian gas to Japan.

The WA government also explained, in its submission, that the first phase of the project ran into major problems.

It said, in the early 1980s, that key players involved in the venture realised that the early contractual agreements would have to be modified because they were threatening to cause SECWA's financial collapse, which could stall (and potentially collapse) the North West Shelf project.

So in March 1985, the Commonwealth and WA governments and the joint venturers agreed to "share the pain" that was forecast to be borne by SECWA, to keep the whole project alive.

Why would the federal government agree to do that?

In his book Inside the Hawke-Keating Government: A Cabinet Diary (2014), Gareth Evans has a story to tell about that.

A North West Shelf 'bombshell'

Mr Evans was one of the major figures in the Hawke and Keating governments of the 1980s and 1990s. He was the minister for Resources and Energy from 1984 to 1987.

His diary entry on January 24, 1985 provides an insight into the politicking that surrounded the gas project at the time.

"A North West Shelf bombshell," his entry began.

"At a hastily arranged late-afternoon meeting in my Canberra office with the Woodside management, led by its managing director, Charles Allen, and chairman, together with Kevan Gosper as the Shell shareholder and a BHP executive as another major shareholder, they tell me a very unhappy story."

Gareth Evans, "Inside the Hawke-Keating Government: A Cabinet Diary", 2014

According to Evans, the executives said they were struggling to secure financing for the project, and they needed to be able to tell a consortium of banks that the SECWA "take or pay" contract for domestic gas purchases would definitely be honoured.

But the WA government, led by premier Brian Burke, was playing a risky political game of brinkmanship, in a bid to get the federal government to tip in financially.

"The immediate Woodside objective is to get us to put pressure on the Burke government to give the necessary assurance, but they acknowledge that some greater role for the Commonwealth — including perhaps picking up the $500 million tab for the West Australian Gas Pipeline — may be required if the whole house of cards is not to collapse," Evans records.

"I indicate that I will raise it with the PM at the first opportunity."

A week later, Evans records that he gets word that the North West Shelf project was in danger of "imminent collapse" and Woodside directors (including Brian Loton from BHP and Kevan Gosper from Shell) were flying to Canberra again to see prime minister Bob Hawke and treasurer Paul Keating.

In another diary entry, he records an episode in which Paul Keating gave Woodside's executives "a fairly withering blast."

"The general theme, which seems to me quite justified, is that they have known about the problem for years, done nothing to resolve it, have been too financially weak to deserve a place in this league, and now — despite all their private enterprise protestations — want the federal government to bail them out so that they can lick bowls of cream into the hereafter," Evans writes of Keating's reprimand.

He records that multiple long days of negotiations were held in February and March between the federal government, WA government, and North West Shelf venture partners, which eventually led to a compromise deal being struck to keep the project above water.

As part of the deal, the federal government agreed to forgo millions of dollars of royalties for a number of years.

Who takes on the risk? Who pays the cost?

Let's return quickly to the WA government's submission to the PRRT inquiry in 2016.

Gas tax inquiry hears arguments for and against An inquiry into the taxation of gas resources has heard from proponents for a tax, who believe Australians are being robbed of their fair share of wealth from the nation's natural resources, and opponents, who argue touching tax settings would spook investors.

As the submission detailed, the WA government supported the North West Shelf project in many other ways, besides the "take-or-pay" contracts.

It said state support included the construction, by SECWA, of the Dampier to Bunbury gas pipeline, at the cost of roughly $1.1 billion, to enable SECWA to deliver the gas it had promised to purchase to major markets in the south-west of WA.

Altogether, it said, WA's expenditure in support of the North West Shelf project was calculated in 2010 by the Western Australian Treasury to exceed $8 billion (in 2010 net present value terms).

"In addition, the Western Australian government incurred costs relating to town site development, schools, hospitals, community facilities and roads that were either directly associated with the project or arising from the economic and population growth accompanying the project," it said. "These costs have never been officially aggregated."

What did Australian Energy Producers claim again?

It claimed (on LinkedIn and Facebook) that "Australia's oil and gas industry relies entirely on private sector investment" and that "in Australia, the private sector — not government — wears all of the risk and up-front costs."

I asked the AEP about those statements on Friday.

In a response, the AEP's chief executive Samantha McCulloch provided this clarified statement:

"Unlike Norway and Qatar, Australian governments do not take an equity stake or invest directly in our oil and gas industry. Instead, we rely on the private sector to invest billions of dollars and carry the full commercial risk of projects. "More than $400 billion has been invested in Australia’s gas industry since 2010 and the sector is the second-biggest corporate taxpayer, paying $21.9 billion in taxes and royalties in 2024–25."

That's a noticeable amendment to the original public claim.

But consider that new line in that new argument that the private sector takes on "the full commercial risk" of projects.

Australian governments help to reduce the commercial risk of major projects by building pipelines and other infrastructure, by signing "take-or-pay" contracts that guarantee long-term demand at certain prices, and so on.

By placing that risk on taxpayers' shoulders, governments take a large amount of risk off the gas industry.

It's why more voters seem to be wondering why Australian governments don't take an ownership stake in these projects.

There's no such thing as a self-made billionaire

At any rate, the North West Shelf project is just one project in Australia. There are many others. When you look into the history of each one, you'll find similar stories.

Which raises a final point.

The AEP originally argued that the private sector in Australia, not governments, wears "all of the risk and up-front costs" of major projects. But that argument relies on a very narrow definition of "risk" and "costs."

What about the cultural costs?

Replica caves in France shaping rebuild of WA's Juukan Gorge Five years after Rio Tinto destroyed a 47,000-year-old sacred rock shelter to expand an iron ore mine, an ambitious rebuild is underway.

When the North West Shelf site was being developed, between 4,000 to 5,000 ancient rock carvings on the Burrup Peninsula were destroyed, and many others were relocated.

In 2020, Rio Tinto infamously destroyed the 46,000-year-old, culturally significant rock shelters in WA's Pilbara so that it could expand its iron ore mine.

What about diplomatic risks and costs?

Do we remember that Australian intelligence officials bugged an East Timorese cabinet office in the early 2000s during negotiations over shared access to the Greater Sunrise oil and gas field, which sits between Australia and East Timor, and an oil and gas treaty worth tens of billions of dollars?

How Australia spied on its poorest neighbour East Timor's most senior leaders accuse Australia of committing a crime and acting immorally after a spying scandal that rocked the relationship between the two countries.

Which industries in Australia were going to benefit from that diplomatic behaviour?

What about the climate risk and the environmental costs?

As former Treasury secretary Ken Henry said recently, Australia is among the top three fossil fuel exporters in the world, and the costs of burning those fossil fuels are being worn by everyone through climate change.

There's no such thing as a self-made billionaire. Private fortunes depend on the social structures and conditions that allow such fortunes to be accumulated.

And the financial success of Australia's export industries depends on the same principle.

World.title: Charles wins over Trump, but fails to impress progressive mayor
World.content:
The US pulled out all the stops for King Charles's state visit with Donald Trump.

Dinner was served on plates encrusted with pure gold. The royal family were heaped with praise. And the King became only the second British monarch to deliver an address to Congress, after his mother Queen Elizabeth II in 1991.

But not everyone was gripped by royal fever.

Newly installed Democratic socialist mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani was elected on a pledge to help the working class.

And on Wednesday (local time) in the city that never sleeps, Mamdani showed exactly what that would look like when it came time to meet the King.

Zohran Mamdani said if he were to speak to the king, he would "probably encourage him to return the Koh-i-Noor diamond". (Reuters: Shannon Stapleton)

The pair both attended a wreath-laying ceremony in the city to honour victims of the 9/11 terrorist attack, but instead of rolling out the red carpet for the monarch, Mamdani's team said the two men would not be meeting privately afterwards.

His spokesman, Joe Calvello, told the New York Times the mayor was "generally opposed to the idea of a king" and when Mamdani was later asked what he would say to Charles if they were to spend time together outside of the ceremony, he didn't mince his words.

"I would probably encourage him to return the Koh-i-Noor diamond," he told reporters.

Mamdani was referencing the most expensive diamond in the world, a precious stone surrendered by — or stolen from, depending on which side is telling the story — a young Indian prince and presented to Queen Victoria in 1850.

Born in Uganda to Indian parents who dedicated their lives to examining colonialism, Mamdani has been more than willing to speak on the issue in the past, most notably when discussing the resistance of Ireland to Britain's "colonial project" in a St Patrick's day speech in March.

With his latest comments he has again shifted attention from the pomp and circumstance of a calculated royal visit to the unsettled question of the Koh-i-Noor's ownership and Britain's colonial legacy.

The debate over a centuries-old diamond

British royal legend says the diamond will bring bad luck to any man who wears it.

Nowadays it mostly sits on display in the Tower of London, set in the front cross of the Queen Mother's Crown.

But many Indians say it belongs to them and have been calling for its return for decades.

Indians seek return of diamond set in royal crown The world's most expensive diamond, the "Kohinoor" is set in the crown made for the Queen Mother. With the passing of Queen Elizabeth II, Indians are asking for its return.

In 2023, after the death of Queen Elizabeth II, those appeals surfaced on social media and reached a fever pitch in the lead up to Charles's coronation.

Queen Camilla chose not to wear the crown with the Koh-i-Noor at the event, opting to reuse another instead, apparently in an effort to avoid scrutiny.

But Mamdani's comments indicate the subject has not been forgotten.

Believed to have originated in the Golconda mines in central southern India, the "Mountain of Light" has a long and complex history.

After it was discovered it was claimed by Mughal Islamic emperors, Sikh maharajahs and emirs of Afghanistan before it ended up in the hands of an 11-year-old Sikh maharajah in the 19th century.

Duleep Singh was leading modern-day Punjab, which was colonised by Britain after two bloody wars that killed thousands, when he signed a peace deal that led to the gem being handed to Queen Victoria.

It has been the subject of myth and intrigue ever since.

"Agatha Christie wrote a book about it and everybody believed it [was stolen]. It wasn't," Melbourne-based jeweller and author Gary Holloway said.

"It survived World War II, [then] it was moved from the Tower of London to Windsor Castle … in a hat box along with a lot of other very famous diamonds, part of the Crown Jewels.

"It was also hidden in a hole dug under the castle walls. Eventually it became part of the Crown Jewels."

Once adorning Queen Mary's crown, the Kohinoor was set in the front middle cross pattée. (Wikimedia Commons: Cyril Davenport )

Mr Holloway said multiple countries with connections to the eighth largest diamond in the world appealed to have the British surrender it.

"It's been kidnapped all through its history," he said.

"Iran wants it, Pakistan wants it, Afghanistan wants it.

" The fact that multiple invaders owned it means India is just one in the chain of people who claim it. "

Since 2000 some Indian politicians have been calling on Britain to return the Koh-i-Noor, seeing its loss as symbolic of the country's subjugation under colonial rule.

"Britain owes us. But instead of returning the evidence of their rapacity to their rightful owners, the British are flaunting the Koh-i-Noor on the Queen Mother's crown in the Tower of London," prominent Indian MP Shashi Tharoor has said.

But just like the debate over countless other treasures taken from other countries during colonial wars that were subsequently put on display in the British Museum, the diamond controversy has not been easily solved.

Royal watchers have pointed out that King Charles doesn't technically own the Koh-i-Noor, and therefore has no more power to return the diamond than he has to hand Buckingham Palace over to the people.

Mamdani snub not the only headline-making moment

King Charles's visit to the United States marked the 250th anniversary of its independence and was designed to help repair the country's "special relationship" with the UK.

Ties between Mr Trump and UK Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer rapidly deteriorated this year because of the latter's reluctance to join the war in Iran.

It was thought King Charles could help smooth things over while in the US given Mr Trump's interest in the royals.

The president's excitement in the lead up to the visit indicated there was merit in the idea. But the trip wasn't without hiccups.

Donald and Melania Trump welcomed King Charles and Queen Camilla to the White House last week. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

Before King Charles touched down in America, maintenance crews plastered lampposts near the White House with the Australian flag instead of the Union Jack.

More consequential were calls from some in parliament for King Charles to cancel the trip after Mr Trump threatened to hit Britain with more tariffs.

Then there was a report in the Financial Times, which obtained audio of remarks made by the new British ambassador to the US, Christian Turner.

Mr Turner said it was "extraordinary" to him that the scandal over Jeffrey Epstein's powerful associates had "brought down a senior member of the royal family, a British ambassador to Washington, potentially the prime minister, and yet here in the US it really hasn't touched anybody".

The comments followed calls for the King to meet with Epstein survivors on this trip, and for him to reference them in his speech to Congress. Charles opted to do neither.

What the King did do was mention three of Mr Trump's most hot-button political issues in the most closely watched event of the visit: his historic address on Capitol Hill to a joint meeting of the Senate and House of Representatives.

NATO, Ukraine and climate change were touched on in quick succession, but Mr Trump didn't seem to mind, describing Charles as an "elegant man" once admired by his late mother.

Loading...

"My mother had a crush on Charles. Can you believe it? Amazing how … I wonder what she's thinking right now," the president said earlier in the week.

Charles, for his part, allowed the president to flatter him. He joked with him at a state dinner on Tuesday about the 1814 British firebombing of the White House and a battle between Britain and France to control North America in the 18th century.

"If it wasn't for us, you'd be speaking French," he quipped.

In his speech to Congress, the King alluded to recent problems in UK-US relations, telling the audience that "we can perhaps agree that we do not always agree".

He also pointed out the two countries had an enduring partnership "born out of dispute".

Meanwhile, Mr Trump avoided mention of any policy disagreements with the Starmer government and largely stuck to script, except when he suggested, without evidence, the King "agrees" with him that Iran should not have nuclear weapons.

But does this mean the special relationship between the US and the UK is repaired?

Trump says 'we'll find out' about mending ties

If history is anything to go by, the special relationship between the UK and the US will not be so easily fixed.

Donald Trump and Sir Keir Starmer at the White House in February 2025. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

Last year Mr Trump stood next to Sir Keir at a White House press conference and praised him for his "beautiful" accent.

He has since mocked his British counterpart, labelled him a "coward" who was "not Winston Churchill" and said he was "not happy with the UK" over its stance on the Iran war.

"It's very sad to see that the relationship is obviously not what it was," Mr Trump told The Sun newspaper last month.

When asked if Charles's visit could improve relations, the US president told the BBC "absolutely, the answer is yes [it could help relations]".

But he appeared to walk that back in comments he made to Sky News last week.

"I can't give you an answer to that," he said.

" I can tell you one thing, our relationship is very good, but you know, that's another individual. We'll find out. "

He added that Sir Keir "has to learn to deal the way [King Charles] deals, and he'll do a lot better".

Certainly both men have had to manage the fallout of similar controversies of late, but what draws Trump to the King, the status of being a royal, his family and their lifestyles, is not easily replicated.

In the meantime, many issues between the two countries remain, including the ongoing fallout of the Iran war and reports the US drafted a proposal to withdraw support for British sovereignty in the Falklands.

At the very least, Sir Keir might be hoping the monarch's visit and soft diplomacy efforts will ease Mr Trump's ire in the short-term.

World.title: 'This is not a game': Survivors disgusted by scam centre simulator games
World.content:
You decide who to abduct.

You decide when to feed them.

You decide how they rip people off to make you money to pay off a debt.

These are key elements of Scam Center Simulator: Under Kingdom (SCS), a computer game made by a man with Australian connections.

It's one of a number of games featuring scam compound scenarios on Steam, the world's biggest PC game distributor.

The ABC approached scam centre victims to get their perspective on the game.

Gavesh, who was unwittingly trafficked to a compound in Myanmar on the promise of a data entry job, was horrified.

"This is not a game, this is our life," he told the ABC, on the condition his real name was not shared.

"They don't know the trauma that we went through, the mental distress that we had to go through. I was really disgusted."

'It was hell'

Gavesh was forced to work in one of South-East Asia's most notorious scam hubs, KK Park, near the Myanmar-Thailand border.

For 16 hours a day, he was forced to run "pig butchering" scams, which involved building fake online profiles using real peoples' photos and videos.

The profiles were used to foster relationships with people online, with the ultimate goal of getting them to invest in sham schemes using cryptocurrency.

Gavesh said KK Park looked like a regular town except it had no bank or police station. (Supplied: Global Alms)

A blurb for SCS on the Steam website says players of the "darkly humorous" game can "use a variety of scam tactics to generate profit, from theft, phishing emails, and manipulating dating apps" to get themselves out of debt.

In the real world, scam compounds are run by organised criminal syndicates that steal tens of billions of dollars from victims each year, according to the UN.

SCS's blurb also says players can control their workers through "punishment" or "re-education".

It's all too familiar for Gavesh, who said workers were not allowed to yawn, talk or sing, and he was hit with a stick for crossing his legs on his second day.

He said a man was left bleeding and unable to stand after being taken to a place called the "water jail," which was known for violent beatings.

"The bosses said, 'If you do not listen to what we say, this is what is going to happen to you.' They showed him as an example for us," he said.

In SCS, players can choose to inflict physical punishment on workers, including electric shocks, and lock them in cages.

Cambodian scam centre had details of 300 Australians Australia's National Anti-Scam Centre says documents seized in a raid on a Cambodian scam compound contained the phone numbers, names and addresses of 300 Australians.

A strict roster was enforced at KK Park to control when Gavesh could eat, sleep and work.

"There were nights that I cried alone in the bed," he said.

"We didn't know if we will be breathing the next day."

His nightmare only ended when he saved enough of his salary to buy his freedom from his bosses, after being locked up in the compound for more than four months.

"It was hell," he said.

He never told his family what happened because he didn't want them to worry, and has since got his life back on track.

After his ordeal, he didn't expect to see the experiences of scam victims like him turned into content for an online game.

The game's developer responds

Romeo Wu is the creator of SCS and was based in Melbourne until recently.

Mr Wu said he made the game after living in South-East Asia for 10 years, where scam centres were "widely discussed".

He told the ABC he wanted "people to find the game fun," but said if it raised awareness about scam compounds "then it would be a positive outcome".

"Indie games often explore unusual or controversial themes, and scam centres are unfortunately a very real issue that affects many people," Mr Wu told the ABC in a statement.

Scam Center Simulator takes visual cues from real scam compounds. (Source: Steam/Jiao Games)

Last year, INTERPOL estimated that hundreds of thousands of people were working in fraud centres in South-East Asia alone.

A UN report published in February found that people in the compounds were subject to "torture, sexual abuse and forced labour".

It is not known exactly how many people have fallen victim to scams run by these centres, or the number of stolen identities they have used.

Mr Wu said he did not speak to any survivors of compounds in research for his game, which was still in beta, adding that it should not "be read as a documentary or a realistic portrayal of individual experiences".

The scam behind the scam Inside the elaborate scam that tricked vulnerable Thai workers into a prison-like Cambodian call centre, forced them to catfish strangers and exposed them to torture.

He said the game did "not glorify fraud or abuse".

"I'm sorry if anyone who has been affected by real scam centres finds the game upsetting, that's not something I take lightly," he said.

"I believe games are a medium, just like films, books, or television. They can explore difficult topics without necessarily endorsing them. My responsibility as a developer is to present these systems honestly, and players also have responsibility in how they interpret them."

Another scam centre survivor, Oak, told the ABC that developers needed to consult with people who had experienced scam compounds to ensure their work educated rather than exploited.

"It feels like our pain is being commodified. Developers profit from a theme that, in reality, destroys lives," said Oak, who also asked to use a pseudonym.

The International Justice Mission (IJM), which helps people who escape scam centres to rebuild their lives, agrees.

"While creative media can be a powerful tool for awareness, we are deeply concerned by the emergence of 'scam centre simulators' that risk gamifying human suffering," IJM's Andrey Sawchenko told the ABC.

"These are not fictional settings; they are sites of real violence and ongoing trauma."

'Media ecology of tragedy'

Blood Money: Lethal Eden is another game on Steam that resembles the scam compounds in Myanmar and Cambodia.

The game, which includes titles in Burmese and Mandarin, sees players follow the story of a character who is drugged by a love interest, before waking up in a cage in a compound surrounded by armed men.

Game developer Jade Flame, based in the Chinese province of Sichuan, did not respond to a request for an interview.

Releasing games on Steam allows creators to dodge China's censorship of video games. (Source: Jade Flame/Steam)

Another game, Escape the Scam Compound, is set for release in 2027 and has been advertised as combining play with "anti-fraud knowledge woven in".

According to the game's Steam blurb, players are lured with "a fake high-paying job" to a scam compound "far from home", where they then work to escape.

Valve Corporation, which owns the Steam platform, did not respond to a request for comment.

Hugh Davies, an associate professor and online game researcher at RMIT University, said: "These specific games sit at the intersection of real-world simulation … horror and political commentary or crisis."

Dr Davies said it was right to question the ethics of these scam centre games, which existed in a "media ecology of tragedy" that included first-person shooter games.

"It's a very niche genre. I think it's part of a media ecology, in the same way that there are a lot of games at the moment that are addressing conflict in the Middle East," he said.

An exodus of Cambodian scam centre survivors created a humanitarian crisis in Phnom Penh earlier this year. (AFP: Tang Chhin Sothy)

Brendan Keogh, an associate professor at the Queensland University of Technology who researches video game production and consumption, said games were good at allowing players to subjectively embody characters within systems that existed in real life.

"It's clearly not necessarily respectful to turn any kind of serious situation into something comedic or entertaining. But that's a broader question that popular culture and media has long grappled with and hasn't found any easy answers to," Dr Keogh said.

Games are not the only media types that have focused on scam centres in recent years.

In March, Netflix released The Red Line, a film that follows the story of scam victims working to track down the people who stole from them.

The 2023 Chinese film No More Bets follows the story of two people who are lured to a compound on the promise of high-paying jobs.

World.title: Danger in the air: Fume events haunt flight crew
World.content:
But across the industry there is scant comprehensive data about the long-term health effects of these fume events on crew. That has left airlines and workers at a stalemate.

For Wakelin, the consequences were substantial. Today, she has no doubt she suffered “aerotoxic syndrome”.

Wakelin had experienced a “fume event” in which she was exposed to oil fumes and their additives, most likely through the plane’s ventilation system.

”I started to feel a bit tired ... I guess my thinking was a bit foggy,” Wakelin says. “At the end of the day I felt like I was almost drunk.”

Anna Wakelin is an active pilot affected by fumes that had an impact on her health. Captain Marcus Diamond is the Australian Federation of Air Pilots safety and technical manager.

When she smelled something like dirty socks she assumed it was the captain playing a practical joke on her. He wasn’t.

In early 2014, Anna Wakelin was flying a Tiger Airways domestic route as part of her certification process to become a captain.

The cabin crew initially noticed “dizziness”, with a “feeling of pressure in the head” and a “metallic taste”, the report said.

That these events can be debilitating is certainly no secret. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau released a report on a June 2023 Sydney-Hobart flight of a Boeing 717 in which flight and cabin crew noticed a “transient chlorine odour” .

And while advanced jet engines are intended to keep cabin air and engine fluids separate, occasionally things go wrong. When that happens, the chemicals can get into the plane’s ventilation systems, resulting in anything from mist or smoke in the cabin to a barely detectable scent. These are classified as “fume events” – a term largely accepted by the industry.

The vast majority of commercial liners today are designed to “bleed” air from the engines, where temperatures hit 2000 degrees C, for use in the interior cabin. When oil gets that hot, it can break down into its constituent chemicals.

One side argues there isn’t a medical definition for “aerotoxic syndrome”. The other fears that they are at the tip of another endemic workplace illness that takes decades to gain recognition, such as asbestosis or silicosis.

But how debilitating these events are, and what symptoms they share, is unclear. The incidence documented by the ATSB resembles Wakelin’s. But Wakelin reported feeling more fatigued and run down in the days after her exposure.

After landing, he experienced a dull headache for two days, the ATSB said.

As the plane approached Hobart airport, the first officer, himself feeling “hazy”, noticed his own reactions slowing as the plane lined up with the runway.

At one point, “the captain noticed quickly developing adverse effects on vision, mental capacity, and movement, and self-assessed as unable to safely fly the aircraft”.

Former airline captain and head of technical standards for the International Federation of Air Line Pilots’ Associations Richard Woodward said: “There is some evidence crew around the world have had neurotoxic poisoning because of pyrolysed oil.” Oil is pyrolysed when its component ingredients are separated by heat. In that process, compounds called organophosphates, used as additives in oil, get released. They are known to cause neurological damage.

The International Air Transport Association, which represents the airlines, says aerotoxic syndrome – the catch-all term for serious illnesses from fume events – “is not a medically or scientifically recognised diagnosis, and there are no scientifically valid tests or treatments”.

Eventually, she was diagnosed with vestibular migraines , which affect balance, ears, and vision.

By April 2014, Wakelin lost her medical certificate for flying, ran through her sick leave and was on Victorian WorkCover. She then received regular payments from the Australian Federation of Air Pilot’s (AFAP) loss-of-licence cover – the pilot-run mutual benefit fund – for six months.

A week later, strapped into the harness in a flight simulator, Wakelin said she couldn’t say which way was up. Her inner ear sense of balance just wasn’t working any more, she said. “I felt like I was just floating through space. It was a bizarre feeling.”

“Days after [the fume event] I was getting more and more fatigued ... I hadn’t cottoned on to the fact that it could have been the aircraft that was making me feel like that.”

Incidents like that have led unions representing flight crews in Australia to see a pattern of topic avoidance by airlines.

Afterwards, the crew member said, “there was definitely pressure” from the airline about how the event was described as either fumes or smell. “We were drawn towards saying it was a smell event to ensure the flight could continue.”

“It was a very strong petrochemical smell … a smell none of us had ever encountered before on an aircraft,” the crew member said.

A member of the Flight Attendant’s Association of Australia told this masthead: “Crew in multiple galleys detected a strong petrochemical odour and some reported headaches.” It was later blamed on lubricant residue on aircraft equipment after maintenance, the crew member said in a statement.

In one example, an Australian cabin crew member reported a fume event on an international flight in the mid-2000s.

Former airline captain and head of technical standards for the International Federation of Air Line Pilots’ Associations Richard Woodward.

Woodward says this issue is a “known problem” but it is typically worse with older planes equipped with older engines.

Yet, they say, as with tobacco and asbestos establishing a cause-and-effect link is not easy.

Fume events put tainted air in a cabin. iStock

Occupational and environmental physician Dr Warren Harrex, a specialist in aerospace medicine, said: “A definitive link has not been established between exposure and long-term health problems.”

“With respect to workers compensation claims, we need to show that an exposure is ‘more likely than not’ to have caused a health problem,” said Harrex, a retired senior RAAF medical officer.

“So this legal threshold for ‘more likely than not’ is unable to be reached for these exposures, because of the absence of good data.”

One well-informed source in the Australian aviation safety sector estimates there would be one to two fume events a month across the entire Australian fleet. The most problematic planes would be the smaller jets used for fly-in, fly-out mining work, primarily in WA.

The source also believes people should worry about both “fume events” and the cumulative effects from the chemicals, which are unknown.

In the US Delta replaced the auxiliary power units on a number of its planes because of fume events. Bloomberg

Industry pushback

The airlines instead point to established safety guidelines and definitions. Qantas Group Chief Health Officer Ian Hosegood said: “Fume or unusual smell events on aircraft are rare.”

When they do occur Qantas crew follow all Australian and international safety guidelines, he said. “We take every report seriously and always act out of an abundance of caution to ensure the health and safety of our crew and customers.” Rex Airlines did not respond to questions on the topic.

Jet engines take in air that is used to ventilate cabins on most jets. iStock

Virgin said the safety and wellbeing of passengers and crew was “our top priority” and that crew were “trained to respond swiftly if a suspected air quality event occurs”.

While “aerotoxic syndrome” is not an official medical term and is not recognised by medical bodies, it is something that has been accepted at various times by governments, unions and courts. A court in France ruled in December that a “direct and essential link” between the neurological illness and the plaintiff’s profession “as an airline pilot was established”.

There is an anecdotal regularity at least. Pilots know when fume events are most likely to occur – when the plane’s engine power is in flux, during take-off or at the start of a descent for landing.

That’s when pressure changes within the engine can result in heated oil being sucked into the air bleed line.

There are signs airlines are aware of the issue. Delta Airlines replaced the auxiliary power units on over 300 Airbus 320s because of air quality issues. (The small engine units provide pneumatic air for onboard air conditioning when the plane is on the ground.)

The Civil Aviation Safety Authority in February republished 2018 information on handling fume events.

Airlines are encouraged to develop procedures guiding in-flight communications, the use of oxygen-masks, and systematic training for crew on the topic.

The science of bleed air

The Flight Attendants’ Association of Australia, in conjunction with AFAP, wants more extensive and systematic testing and reporting into air quality in aircraft – the kind that can capture data on fume events and the health impact on crew.

Yet consistent, truly comprehensive data showing the frequency and severity of fume events is scarce.

Dr Harrex believes what’s needed is a comprehensive registry, so that anyone who reports exposure can have their case added to it. However, registries cost money to maintain, especially when events are infrequent. So it’s probably beyond the capability of any one airline, he said.

Yet one of the thorniest aspects of the issue of tainted air stems from the design of most commercial aircraft, which use “bleed air”.

Bleed air design goes back to the Boeing B-52 jet bomber. AP

“Bleed air” is used not just to help keep the plane pressurised and with enough oxygen but also to keep the cabin at the right temperature, UNSW senior lecturer in aerospace design Sonya Brown said. At about 36,000 feet, the outside temperature is -56.5 degrees.

“If we removed bleed air, we can’t actually get to the temperature requirements easily without using a lot more energy,” she said.

Modern “bleed air” systems are based on the 1950s B-52 bomber design. The bomber’s design formed the template for the shape of commercial aircraft for decades to come.

A spokesperson for Boeing said the company had a long history of supporting industry efforts to assess air quality but the world’s leading aerospace medical associations “have rejected a connection between cabin air and significant health effects, and no aviation regulator has determined that additional safety regulations are required”.

Boeing nevertheless “continues to work with scientists to improve our understanding of cabin environmental factors”, the spokesperson said.

Boeing rival Airbus said its planes were designed and manufactured according to all airworthiness requirements and the company worked with operators and regulators to ensure the best possible cabin environment for passengers and crew.

The air intake on the fuselage of the Boeing 787, the only commercial jet that doesn’t use bleed air from the engines to pressurise, heat and cool the cabin. The Age

AFAP wants to see “bleed air” systems avoided in future aircraft design. And yet, with its efficiencies, “bleed air” is the default design for most commercial aircraft.

Perhaps it’s for this reason that AFAP’s Safety & Technical Manager Captain Marcus Diamond said that discussions with the ATSB on the issue historically don’t go very far.

“Imagine them saying that all the current modern fleet of airliners have got a design fault in their bleed system. They just won’t do it.”

It’s Boeing, actually, that carries the distinction as the only aircraft maker to create a major plane that doesn’t have the bleed-air system on engines.

The 787 Dreamliner instead uses pumps on the fuselage to bring air in and then to circulate it from there. This involves extra weight and power requirements for the plane.

The approach of the airlines and plane-makers continues to raise suspicions of affected employees.

Wakelin, the former Tiger Airways pilot, said that what was disturbing was her employer’s response to the case. The airline told her essentially that “I was making it up and that I should keep quiet and not talk about it”.

A spokesperson for Virgin, which was in the process of acquiring Tiger Airways Australia from Singapore-based Tiger Airways Holdings in 2014, addressed the incident saying: “The safety and wellbeing of our guests and crew is our top priority.”

”Extensive research shows the air inside commercial aircraft is of high-quality and meets relevant international air quality standards.”

After Wakelin was told by her doctor that she would likely never go back to flying, she began studying for a new career in law. But she actively tried to regain her medical qualification to fly.

After two years, she began to see an improvement with treatment. “I was very lucky.” Wakelin eventually got her medical qualification back and returned to flying with a different airline.

While Woodward, the former captain, acknowledges the issue of sickening fume events, he believes flying is “safe for regular passengers” and suspects “the amount of contamination regular passengers would see would be minimal”.

Dr Harrex, the occupational safety expert, agrees, saying passengers don’t likely face long-term problems from the risk. “For people who are employed as cabin crew who might be getting more exposures, there is a possibility it may lead to long-term consequences.”

“Just because we can’t prove that a health problem may be caused by exposure, or deny that it may be related to the exposure, workers still need to be treated,” said Dr Harrex.

“Their symptoms and illnesses are real and they need to be managed regardless of the causation.”
